title: Low-level and object-oriented design
subtitle: Learn a repeatable method for designing the classes of a small system, carried through one parking lot, from the first question to the race at two gates.

c.v: This story is made up, but the pattern is common. Ravi had a 45-minute low-level design round. The prompt was one line: "Design a parking lot."

At minute 30 the interviewer asked, "Two cars arrive at two gates at the same moment. Can both get spot 14?" Ravi looked at his code. Both gates read the spot as free, then both took it. He had no answer.
Then came the second question: "We want different prices for trucks." The price logic sat in four methods of the manager. He had to edit all four.
The feedback said: "Knows the patterns. Did not clarify
. Design breaks under change and under concurrent use." Ravi had written more code than the strong candidates. It was the wrong code.

A low-level design (LLD) round gives you a small, self-contained problem. You design its classes, their methods and how they work together. Hello Interview puts it this way: these rounds "test your ability to structure code for a self-contained problem". The round is also called object-oriented design.
for scale. In an LLD round, you design the inside of one program. Hello Interview's summary: "System design is the map. Low level design is the blueprint for a building on the map."
Interviewers judge five things: how you analyse the problem, your class design, code quality, how easily the design takes a follow-up change, and how you explain it.
Code quality includes choosing composition or inheritance, managing state and the direction of dependencies.

Hello Interview's framework has five steps, about 35 minutes in total.
Here is a version you can repeat.
The prompt is vague on purpose. Your job is to "turn it into a spec you can actually design around".

For the parking lot, Hello Interview picks a sample scope. There are three vehicle types: motorcycle, car and large vehicle. Entry gives a free, compatible spot and a ticket. Exit takes the ticket, works out the fee and frees the spot. The price is hourly, rounded up.
Payments, gate hardware, cameras, the UI and reservations are out of scope.
Say that list out loud. It protects your time.
2. Find the core objects and their responsibilities
Pull out the meaningful nouns from your requirements.
For the parking lot: lot, spot, ticket, vehicle. But "don't turn every noun into a class. Some things are just data."
Give each object one job, in one sentence:
: takes cars in and out, and owns the spots and the active tickets.
: knows its size and whether it is taken.
: records which vehicle is in which spot, and since when.
: just data, a plate and a size.
The framework's rule: "keep rules with the entity that owns the relevant state."
Fowler calls the same habit tell-don't-ask: "rather than asking an object for data and acting on that data, we should instead tell an object what to do."
So the lot tells a spot "take this ticket". It does not read a

You have about 10 minutes for code. Start with the happy path, then the edge cases.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: In a design review or a
, ask each new class "What is your one job?" If the answer has "and" three times, it needs a split.
: a manager or service that keeps growing. Refactoring.Guru notes that classes "usually start small" but bloat as the program grows.
Look for objects that are only getters and setters, with all rules in a service. Fowler calls this an
. He calls it "really just a procedural style design".
Move the rule next to the data it reads.

Do not chase getters everywhere, though. Fowler himself says, "personally, I don't use tell-dont-ask". He still puts data and behaviour together, but he has seen the rule push people to remove every getter.
When you see a new abstract base class, ask what behaviour the subclasses change. If none, suggest a field.
When you see a new interface, ask for the second implementation. If nobody can name it, wait. Hello Interview says: "Build what you need now, not what you might need later."
For every shared object, ask: "What if two requests call this at once?" Look for a read, a decision and a write as three separate lines.
"Here is my parking lot spec and its out-of-scope list. Propose the classes, with one sentence of responsibility each. Do not add any design pattern I did not ask for."
"In this class design, find every place where code reads a value, decides, then writes it back in a separate step. For each, say what two threads could do to break it."
"List the classes in this diff that only have getters and setters. For each, name the service method that holds its rules."
The agent did not turn every noun into a class or add subclasses that change no behaviour.
Every pattern it added solves a change you can name.
The concurrency fix makes the check and the action one atomic step. A
method that only wraps the check is not a fix.
The code compiles and a test with two threads passes many times in a row.

q.v: An LLD interviewer says "Design a parking lot." What should you do in the first few minutes?

options.v: Draw the full class diagram with every vehicle type you can think of.
Ask questions until the prompt is a small spec, and say what is out of scope.
Pick the design patterns you will use, so the interviewer sees them early.

why.v: Hello Interview's framework starts with about 5 minutes of requirements, where you make the prompt unambiguous and name what is out of scope.

q.v: Car, Motorcycle and Truck differ only in which spot size they need. How should you model them?

options.v: One Vehicle type with a size field, because there is no different behaviour.
An abstract Vehicle class with three subclasses, so you can add more later.
A VehicleFactory and a Vehicle interface with three classes.

why.v: Subclasses that add no behaviour are inheritance used as labels. A field holds the difference, and a new size is one enum value.

q.v: Two gates call enter() at the same moment. Both see spot 14 as free and both issue a ticket for it. What is the root problem?

options.v: The spot list is not sorted.
Checking "is it free?" and taking the spot happen as two separate steps.
The ticket IDs are not unique.

why.v: This is check-then-act. Another thread can change the state between the check and the action, so the two must happen as one atomic step.

q.v: The interviewer asks for different prices for cars and trucks. Which change fits best?

options.v: Add an if on vehicle size inside ParkingLot.exit().
Put the fee rule behind a small PricingPolicy interface that ParkingLot calls.
Make CarTicket and TruckTicket subclasses of Ticket.

why.v: Pricing is now a real change pressure, so it earns a seam. ParkingLot keeps one job, and a new price rule is a new class.
